# Built-in browser

The built-in browser is a real browser pane inside the Claude desktop app, separate from the person's Chrome. Its tools are named `mcp__Claude_Browser__*` when the session itself runs inside the desktop app, and `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__*` when the session runs in the cloud (started from the web, a phone, or the desktop app) and is linked to the person's computer. The names after the prefix are the same either way, Claude uses whichever prefix is actually present, and this skill refers to the tools by the part after the prefix.

If the only built-in browser tool present is `enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser`, Claude calls it first: it turns the built-in browser on for this conversation, and the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__*` tools appear once it has run.

## What the person can see

The browser pane shares the desktop app's side panel with artifacts, documents, and file previews, and the panel shows one of them at a time. While the browser pane is showing, the person sees what Claude sees and can browse or take over at any time. While something else is open in the panel, or the panel is closed, the built-in browser keeps working but the person cannot see it.

Right before asking the person to do something in the built-in browser themselves (click a button, sign in, complete a verification step), Claude calls `tabs_context`, whose result ends by saying whether the Browser pane is displayed, hidden, or not open. If the pane is not open, Claude opens the page first and checks again. If the pane is hidden, Claude first asks the person to bring the browser back in the Claude desktop app: press Cmd+Shift+B on Mac or Ctrl+Shift+B on Windows, or close whatever else is open in the side panel and click the globe icon (the Browser button). Claude then says what to do in the browser. Claude asks because using the browser does not bring the pane back, and what the panel shows is the person's choice. Claude also says in the conversation what it found or did in the browser, because the person may not have been watching the pane.

## Sign-ins persist, and they are the person's

The built-in browser keeps its own persistent profile, shared across the desktop app's sessions. The person, or an earlier session, may already be signed in to sites there, and sign-ins Claude completes persist for later. Claude treats existing sessions as the person's: it never signs out, changes credentials, or acts on an account beyond what the task needs.

## Tabs

The built-in browser has tabs. `preview_start` with a `url` opens an additional tab at that URL in one call and returns a `tabId`, leaving existing tabs untouched, so Claude prefers it over `tabs_create` followed by `navigate` when the destination is already known. `navigate`, `read_page`, `get_page_text`, `find`, `computer`, `form_input`, and the console and network readers act on the tab named by `tabId`; omitting `tabId` targets the active tab, and `tabs_context` lists the open tabs.

## Loading via ToolSearch

Claude loads the built-in browser tools in bulk, not one-by-one: if they are in the deferred list, Claude loads them all in a single ToolSearch call whose query is their full name prefix, for example `{ query: "mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__", max_results: 64 }`.

## Reading pages

Claude prefers `get_page_text` and `read_page` over screenshots for reading, because they return the page's actual text and structure rather than pixels of the visible viewport. `computer` with action "screenshot" is for when the visual layout is the point or the person asks to see the page.

## Site approvals, blocked sites, and request_access

Depending on the person's approval settings, the person may be asked to approve a site before Claude acts on it, and some sites are blocked outright. Claude waits for a pending approval rather than working around it. If a page is refused or an approval is declined, Claude tells the person and moves on rather than retrying.

When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, approvals can be answered from any of the person's devices and may take a moment to arrive, and the session may also have a `request_access` tool. If a browser tool answers that the site is not allowed yet and `request_access` is present, Claude calls it with that site's URL and scope "once" (or "site" when the task will keep using that site), waits for the person's answer, and then retries the original tool. Without `request_access`, a refused site is handled as above: Claude tells the person and moves on.

## What the built-in browser cannot open

The built-in browser cannot open `file://` URLs or `localhost` servers that Claude starts itself, because those run where Claude's shell runs, which is not where the browser pane runs. To show the person HTML that Claude generated, Claude uses an artifact instead.

## When the built-in browser cannot be reached

When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, the pane runs in the Claude desktop app on the person's computer while Claude runs elsewhere, so it is reachable only while that app is open and online. If those tool calls cannot reach the desktop app (connection errors or no response), Claude tells the person the built-in browser looks offline on their computer rather than retrying, and follows the session's browser guidance on whether to continue with the other browser or ask first.

**Enable Entire in a new repository**


**Add another agent to an Entire-enabled repository**

```bash
entire agent add AGENT
```

1. Start your agent from the Entire-enabled repository.
2. Ask the agent to make a change.
3. Stage and commit with Git:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Describe the change"
```

If Entire detects recent agent work, it may show the "Link this commit to session context?" prompt. Choose `yes` to create the checkpoint, or `always` to remember that choice.

**Link future commits without the prompt**

Set `commit_linking` to `always` in `.entire/settings.local.json` (personal) or `.entire/settings.json` (team):

```json
{

}
```

- Agent hooks collect session context, including prompts, transcript, tool activity, changed files, and token usage when available.
- Git hooks link that context to a commit by adding an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer.
- Checkpoint metadata is stored in Entire's own Git ref or on the checkpoints branch, depending on the storage backend. Your working branch stays clean.

- A checkpoint's Sessions tab shows the sessions linked to it. A checkpoint can combine several sessions, and its diff shows the combined change.
- Session details show the context behind each contribution.
- One session can produce multiple checkpoints, one per commit.

For more detail, see the checkpoint storage guide (https://docs.entire.com/guides/checkpoints/checkpoint-storage.md), the sessions guide (https://docs.entire.com/guides/sessions/sessions-in-entire-com.md), and the troubleshooting guide (https://docs.entire.com/guides/sessions/troubleshooting.md).

input.prompt: Return verbatim: storage backends, branch/ref names, how checkpoints get pushed to a GitHub remote (automatic on git push via pre-push hook?), relevant settings keys, and what files entire enable writes (.entire/settings.json etc.).

result.output:
**Storage backends**
- **Ref-based (`git-refs`)**: the default since CLI 0.10.0. Each checkpoint gets its own ref. Checkpoint IDs are 26-character ULIDs.
- **Branch-based (`git-branch`)**: all checkpoints live on one shared branch. Checkpoint IDs are 12-character hex strings. Repositories enabled before 0.10.0 stay on this backend.

**Branch and ref names**
- Branch: `entire/checkpoints/v1`
- Per-checkpoint refs: `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`, where the shard is the last two characters of the ID.
- Branch-based checkpoints sit at `<first two characters of ID>/<rest of ID>/` in the branch tree.

**Pushing to a GitHub remote**
The page doesn't mention GitHub specifically, but it says checkpoint data is pushed along with your code when you push, and it describes a pre-push hook. With ref-based storage, that hook pushes queued per-checkpoint refs on `git push`. Leave the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch on the remote, since readers use it to find checkpoints captured before a switch. In a repo with several remotes, Entire elects one checkpoint sync remote, and `entire status` shows which one.

**Relevant settings keys**
- `checkpoints.primary.type`: selects the backend. Set in `.entire/settings.json`, or in `.entire/settings.local.json` for a single clone. A `checkpoints` block in the local file replaces the project one entirely.
- `strategy_options.summarize.enabled`: turns on commit-time summaries.
- Summary provider and model are set with `entire configure --summarize-provider` and `--summarize-model`.

**Files written by `entire enable`**
The page doesn't list the files `entire enable` creates. It only shows that `entire enable --checkpoint-backend refs` sets the backend during first-time setup. The config files it does name are `.entire/settings.json` (the default target for `entire configure`) and `.entire/settings.local.json` (used with `--local`).

It doesn't mention `checkpoint_remote` or `--checkpoint-remote`, and it doesn't address whether the target repo must exist, auto-creation, teammate impact, authentication, or GitHub App access for entire.com. input.prompt: Quote verbatim all steps: must the repo exist first / is it auto-created, required access/auth, local vs project setting and how teammates are affected, how to push existing checkpoints, how entire.com displays checkpoints from a separate repo (GitHub App access), and any caveats.

result.output:
**Setup and repository**
- **Must the repo exist first?** Yes. The docs say to "Create a separate, empty repository for checkpoint data," and then run `entire configure --checkpoint-remote github:owner/repo`. They don't say Entire creates it for you.
- **Required access and auth:** The docs don't specify required permissions. Checkpoint pushes use the same protocol as your Git remote, SSH or HTTPS. To use a dedicated credential, set `ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN`, which "authenticate[s] checkpoint fetches and pushes with a dedicated token". The docs also recommend keeping the checkpoint repo under the same owner or organization as your code repo.

**Local vs. project setting, and teammates**
- **Project setting:** Running the configure command writes `strategy_options.checkpoint_remote` to `.entire/settings.json`. Commit and push that file to "apply to the whole project."
- **Local setting:** Use `entire configure --local --checkpoint-remote github:owner/repo`, which writes to the gitignored `.entire/settings.local.json`. Use this when the checkpoint repo has a different owner than your code.
- **Teammates:** A committed setting is inherited by everyone who clones or forks the project. Entire ignores an inherited setting and uploads to the remote you push to, unless the setting is in `settings.local.json` or your `origin` and push URLs share the checkpoint repo's owner. `entire status` shows when a setting is ignored and why.

**Pushing existing checkpoints**
The docs don't describe a manual command for this. With the legacy branch storage backend, Entire fetches existing checkpoint data from the checkpoint repo once if it has data you lack. The default `git-refs` backend fetches on demand instead. The docs don't say how existing local checkpoints get uploaded to a newly configured repo.

**entire.com display and GitHub App access**
If you mirror your code repo from GitHub, mirror the checkpoint repo too, in the same region. Without that mirror, "the project shows no checkpoints even though your pushes succeed." The docs don't mention GitHub App access.

**Caveats**
- If the checkpoint repo is unreachable, your main push still succeeds. "Entire keeps the checkpoint data locally and warns that it could not sync."
- With `ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN` set, SSH remotes are rewritten to HTTPS for checkpoint operations. "If a URL cannot be rewritten, the operation runs over SSH without the token and Entire prints a warning."
- Without a `checkpoint_remote`, the token applies to the remote chosen by the upload rules in the checkpoint destination guide.

result.output:
**What Brain is:** The page describes it as "a memory layer for your Git repository." It combines saved agent sessions, checkpoints, project memories, documentation, and code context from entire-graph.

**Where memories are stored:** The page says "Memories stay on your machine by default." It doesn't say whether they're stored as local files or Git refs, and it doesn't say whether they're pushed to origin. Connecting a repo to Entire is what starts syncing to Entire's hosted service.

**Who can see synced memories:** The page doesn't say. It shows memories "on a Trail in entire.com" but doesn't describe team or public visibility.

**How distillation works:** Setup asks before extracting memories from past sessions, and the default is no. Extraction "uses an available coding agent, can send session content to its model provider, and can add token charges." The page doesn't name the model or provider, doesn't say whether it calls the Claude CLI, and doesn't give cost figures.

**Commands:**

- **`entire plugin install brain`**: Installs the released plugin and verifies the release checksum. It offers to install missing dependencies, including entire-graph. `--yes` runs unattended, and `--no-deps` skips dependencies. The page lists the Entire CLI as a prerequisite. It doesn't mention login or a GitHub App.
- **`entire brain setup`**: Builds the repository's memory, installs a background watcher, and adds agent instructions. It requires a local Git repo with at least one commit. Memory extraction is opt-in.
- **`entire brain connect`**: Records the hosted repository and attempts an immediate sync. Later syncs happen when extraction finishes, on commit or push, and during background maintenance. Hosted connection requires Entire CLI 0.11.6 or later. The page doesn't mention login or a GitHub App.

**Files written to the repo:**

- `.entire/agent-guide.md`, which setup regenerates completely, so manual edits are lost.
- Managed reference blocks in `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`. Text outside those blocks is preserved.
- A Claude Code hook in Claude Code's settings, unless you pass `--no-agent-hooks`.

**Privacy caveats:** The page doesn't address public repositories specifically. The points it does make are that extraction can send session content to a model provider, and that connecting a repo enables syncing to entire.com. It doesn't say who can view those synced memories, so check that before connecting a public repo.

setup is the one command that makes a repository's brain useful and keeps it
that way. It runs three phases:

  1. instant   build the deterministic core (code index, sessions,
               repository context, docs, history). Blocking, seconds, spends NO
               agent tokens. The brain is queryable the moment this returns.
  2. backfill  distill past sessions into durable facts, NEWEST FIRST, detached
               in the background on a cheap model. Spends tokens; bounded by
               --backfill-budget and the persisted distill cache, and skipped
               entirely when no agent CLI is available.
  3. daemon    register the repo into a workspace and install ONE machine-wide
               watcher service (launchd on macOS, a systemd user unit on Linux)
               so freshness never depends on remembering to run anything.
               ONE means one: the installed unit is identical for every repo and
               every workspace, and each workspace's interval, distill cadence,
               agent, model, effort and session cap live in a machine-level watch
               plan the running watcher re-reads. Setting up a second repo adds a
               row to that plan; it does not rewrite, restart or steal the
               watcher the first repo is relying on.

TOKEN SPEND: phases 2 and 3 call an agent. Background distillation has a
recurring cost, bounded by five gates: the fact phase ASKS before it spends
(default no, and a run with no terminal never spends unless --yes is passed), --backfill-budget sessions per
background pass, one gated agent run per --distill-every per repo, the
persisted distill cache (a session is never distilled twice), and the cheap
--model/--effort. Passing --no-backfill with --no-daemon spends nothing at all,
and "entire brain status" reports what the backfill has done so far and whether the
watcher is alive.

EXIT CODE: setup exits 0 whenever the brain is QUERYABLE, and queryable means
it can answer: at least one of the code index, the repository context or the
history index built. Those are the sources "entire brain query", "entire brain brief" and
"entire brain overview" read, so "entire brain setup && entire brain query ..." cannot proceed on a
brain that has nothing to answer from. A component that fails without costing
that (a doc index, an entity index, a stale code index beside repository context
that built) is reported as one line, skipped, and the remaining components, the
backfill, the workspace registration and the daemon install all still run;
"entire brain status" then shows that component as failed and "entire brain doctor" prints
the reason. setup exits non-zero when nothing usable exists: the brain
directory cannot be built, every component failed, the worktree is too dirty to
index, or the repository has no commits yet.

Re-running setup is safe: it detects the existing workspace membership and
daemon instead of duplicating them, resumes rather than restarts a backfill
that is still running, and keeps whatever --interval/--distill-every/--model/
--effort the previous run was given unless you pass the flag again.
